## Appendix 1. Extended literature review

The Introduction describes two ways in which the artifacts of a study fail to describe it. Some decisions are stated in no artifact, and copies of other decisions drift apart. This appendix first reviews the evidence for both across the four stages of a study. It then reviews the approaches that address parts of the problem, from workflow engines and experiment builders to evaluation harnesses for artificial agents, and closes with the design principles that these findings imply (@reltbl-principles).

### Evidence across the stages of a study

**Design.** Preregistration fixes decisions before the data are seen, but a plan written in prose can still leave them open. In a comparison of 53 preregistrations, a structured template restricted researchers' freedom more than an unstructured one, yet neither format removed it. Coders agreed on the number of hypotheses in only 14% of the plans [@bakker2020preregistrations]. Adoption of preregistration and of other transparency practices also remains limited [@hardwicke2024prevalence].

**Run.** A Methods section is meant to let others repeat a procedure, but audits find that it often cannot. Across 241 fMRI articles, many did not report critical details of the experimental design, data acquisition, or analysis [@carp2012secret]. When the Reproducibility Project in cancer biology set out to repeat 193 experiments, none was described in enough detail to design a replication protocol from the paper alone, so the original authors had to be asked for clarification [@errington2021challenges]. The large replication project in psychology likewise used the original materials whenever they were available, rather than rebuilding each study from its published description [@osc2015]. Details that a Methods section treats as incidental can also change what participants experience, because the same experiment runs with different timing precision depending on the software, the operating system, and the browser [@bridges2020timing; @anwylirvine2021timing].

**Analyze.** Analysis decisions are among the most consequential and the least fixed in advance. Undisclosed flexibility in data collection and analysis can make almost any result significant [@simmons2011falsepositive], and the same data processed in different reasonable ways can support different conclusions [@steegen2016multiverse]. Given one question and one dataset, 29 teams returned odds ratios from 0.89 to 2.93 [@silberzahn2018manyanalysts], and 70 teams analyzing one neuroimaging dataset used no two identical workflows [@botviniknezer2020variability]. Sharing the data does not settle the analysis either. Of 35 articles with open data, only 11 could be reproduced without help from their authors, and 13 could not be fully reproduced even with that help [@hardwicke2018cognition]. Of 14 articles with open data badges, only six shared their analysis code, and only one could be reproduced exactly [@cruwell2023badge].

**Report.** Even when a plan is registered, the published report often departs from it without saying so. Of 67 clinical trials whose outcome reporting was audited, only nine reported their outcomes faithfully [@goldacre2019compare]. Of 27 studies published with a Preregistered badge between 2015 and 2017, 25 deviated from their preregistration, mostly in sample size, exclusion criteria, and statistical analysis, and only one disclosed all of its deviations [@claesen2021adherence]. Reporting guidelines do not close the gap on their own. In a randomized trial of 1689 manuscripts submitted to a journal, asking authors to complete the ARRIVE checklist did not improve compliance with the guidelines, and no manuscript in either group complied fully [@hair2019iicarus]. More generally, endorsing a guideline is not the same as following it [@percie2020arrive]. Psychological Science now makes transparency the default and has editors check it [@hardwicke2024transparency], and current guidance asks authors to list their deviations from a preregistration by hand [@willroth2024deviations].

Taken together, these findings suggest that the gaps follow less from careless authors than from describing a process in prose, where nothing marks a decision as missing and nothing keeps the copies of a decision in agreement. Studyflow gives each decision a place in one diagram, which makes a missing value easy to catch, and every audience reads a view of that one diagram (Results).

### Workflow engines

Studyflow can be read as a workflow modeling approach. Such approaches differ along three axes. An approach may define a process or execute it, may serve any domain or one [@zhao2008scientific_workflows], and may model control flow or data flow [@cuevasvicenttin2013workflows]. Control-flow systems model what happens, and data-flow systems model which data are derived from which. A study needs both. It has a procedural flow of conditions, phases, and steps, and a data flow from raw to cleaned to analyzed data. A Studyflow diagram therefore carries both over one shared set of nodes, which few systems offer in one artifact.

Graphical platforms such as Galaxy [@thegalaxycommunity2024] and KNIME [@berthold2009] made analysis pipelines easier to compose. Modern engines, among them Nextflow [@nextflow], Snakemake [@wirth2024], Kedro [@kedro], and Nipype and Pydra [@pydra], model a process as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and run it at scale. The Common Workflow Language [@cwl] makes pipelines portable and declarative. In psychology, reproducible practice wraps the analysis in code, containers, and build tools [@peikert2021reproducible], and continuous integration tools have been repurposed for analysis [@beaulieujones2017continuous].

Most of these tools are written for machines and developers. They model a workflow as a DAG with fixed inputs and require programming skills that ethics review panels, reviewers, and many collaborators do not have. A study, by contrast, is iterative and cyclic [@ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. Piloting revises the design, sessions repeat, and a preregistered sequential design can send a researcher back to collect more data [@lakens2014sequential]. Agentic AI frameworks met the same limit, because applications of language models need cycles, state, and human interrupts [@langgraph2024]. Studyflow keeps these loops in the study model, much as statecharts made the states of a complex system readable in one diagram [@harel1987statecharts], and hands each external computation to the toolkit built for it.

The machine learning community has described the failures of implicit coordination as "glue code" and "pipeline jungles", in which changing anything changes everything [@sculley2015hidden]. Seven tool families evolved independently, namely build systems, CI/CD (the automated building and testing of software), data and machine learning orchestrators, scientific workflow systems, provenance standards, experiment trackers, and agent frameworks. All arrived at broadly the same primitives, which are typed steps, named data artifacts, directed graphs, and provenance. This convergence suggests that the primitives answer a general need rather than the habits of one community. Studyflow adopts these primitives and adds what none of these families expresses, the study itself. Its diagram states the between-subjects design, the assignment of participants, the consent step, and the preregistered hypotheses.

Two of Studyflow's file conventions, a text form with one line per attribute and a diagram embedded in its exported image, have precedents outside research. Configuration as code is standard practice in CI/CD, yet a study of failing GitHub Actions workflows found YAML misconfigurations that often surface only when the workflow runs [@zheng2025actionsfail]. Studyflow keeps the YAML and adds a validating schema, which catches such errors before a run, and a visual view kept in step with the text. Embedding the source in an exported image makes it shareable between technical and non-technical audiences. Every image that a ComfyUI pipeline generates, for example, carries its full workflow, so sharing a reproducible pipeline amounts to sharing a picture [@comfyui2023].

### Experiment builders and orchestration platforms

A separate ecosystem specifies and runs the behavioral experiment itself. Libraries and builders such as PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy], jsPsych [@deleeuw2015jspsych], lab.js [@henninger2022labjs], OpenSesame [@mathot2012opensesame], and the online platform Gorilla [@anwylirvine2020gorilla] implement tasks and studies. Orchestration platforms run whole online studies. Among them, oTree [@chen2016otree] and Empirica [@almaatouq2021empirica] support interactive designs, Deliberate Lab runs real-time experiments with people and AI agents [@tessler2025deliberatelab], Dallinger and PsyNet run complex automated timelines [@harrison2026psynet], Pushkin serves very large online cohorts [@hartshorne2019pushkin], and the Experiment Factory deploys many cognitive tasks in containers [@sochat2018expfactory].

A design layer is also emerging. SweetPea compiles declarative factorial designs into stimulus sequences [@musslick2022sweetpea], AutoRA closes the loop between design, data collection, and model discovery [@musslick2024autora], and SweetBean compiles one declarative stimulus specification into a jsPsych experiment for people or a text experiment for language models [@strittmatter2025sweetbean]. Neuroscience has gone furthest toward machine-readable tasks. BEADL specifies the state machine of a single trial in validated XML [@beadl], and Bonsai [@lopes2015bonsai], pyControl [@akam2022pycontrol], and Autopilot [@saunders2019autopilot] drive the experimental apparatus from formal task descriptions.

Each of these tools specifies or runs one part of a study, such as a stimulus sequence, the state machine of a trial, or a deployment, in code or in a tool-specific builder. Several do so more expressively than Studyflow. Studyflow supplies the consent, eligibility, allocation, data format, and reporting around a task authored in one of them.

### Reporting guidelines and protocol registries

Experimental protocols are shared as free text, through registries such as protocols.io [@teytelman2016] or as supplements to manuscripts. The EQUATOR network [@simera2010equator] catalogs reporting guidelines, among them CONSORT for randomized trials [@hopewell2025consort], SPIRIT for protocols, first published in 2013 and updated in 2025 [@spirit2013; @chan2025spirit], CHART for evaluations of chatbots [@chart2025], STROBE [@strobe], STARD [@stard], PRISMA [@page2021prisma], and TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier]. Several of them standardize flow diagrams [@egger2001]. These guidelines impose structure only when the study is reported. They store it in free-text fields and in document formats such as PDF or DOCX, and they give no representation of the procedure that a machine can run or check.

Executable publishing approaches the same problem from the publisher's side. eLife's Executable Research Articles make the analysis live and runnable inside the published paper [@maciocci2019era; @tsang2020era], and hypothesis tests written as code make the statistical prediction checkable [@lakens2021machinereadable]. The experimental procedure that produced the data, however, remains in prose.

### Data standards and ontologies

Community standards such as BIDS [@bids] and its extensions [@pernet2019eegbids], Psych-DS [@psychds], CSVW [@csvw], and the Behaverse Data Model [@bdm], together with the FAIR principles [@fair], prescribe how datasets are organized. Related efforts structure analysis outputs and methods reporting, such as NIDM-Results [@maumet2016nidm] and ARTEM-IS, from its design guidelines [@styles2021artemis] to its reporting template for EEG methods [@soskic2025artemis]. All of them make the data or their products machine-readable, but they say little about the process that produced the data. Studyflow describes that process and refers to these standards for the data themselves.

### Provenance and packaging

Another line of work pins the computational environment so that an analysis runs again identically. Package managers such as conda and pip, container images such as Docker and Singularity, and job managers that run each experiment in a container, such as Caliban [@ritchie2020], freeze software dependencies. They capture the environment in which the code runs, not the experimental procedure that produced the data. The W3C PROV standard defines a vocabulary for provenance, that is, where data came from and which process produced them [@w3cprov]. RO-Crate packages research artifacts with their metadata for FAIR exchange and archiving [@soilandreyes2022rocrate], and Workflow Run RO-Crate records runs of computational workflows [@leo2024wfrunrocrate]. Systems such as Science Capsule record which software produced which output [@ghoshal2021; @souza2020provenance], and process mining recovers process models from runtime traces [@vanderaalst2016process].

These approaches describe what was run after the fact. They track the computation but rarely the experimental context, such as eligibility decisions, randomization, manual annotations, protocol deviations, or the behavior of a participant [@simmons2018provenance_sport]. Studyflow complements them. It is a specification written before the run, and these standards can package its runs.

### Visual notations

Box-and-arrow figures show the logic of a study at a glance, but they are often not standardized, rarely connected to code, and usually drawn for one audience, such as a CONSORT flow for a journal, a slide for a funding agency, or a sketch for an engineer [@bogale2024]. Adjacent fields have standardized graphical notations, notably the Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009]. Efforts to document and visualize workflows for communication and publication point in the same direction [@willoughby2017], yet no such notation targets experimental cognitive science.

BPMN [@bpmnspec] itself has been used for clinical pathways and research workflows [@braun2014; @dhond2021projectflow; @knight2024visualizing; @pufahl2022; @zarour2019], serverless machine learning [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], collaboration between humans and agents [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent], organizational modeling [@guerreiro2024], and process simulation [@cimino2025]. It has mature tools, such as bpmn-js [@bpmnjs], and tools that generate executable workflow code from a drawn diagram [@diagrid]. Recent authoring tools based on large language models, such as ProMoAI [@kourani2024promoai] and conversational modeling [@kopke2025], speed up drafting, but fluent syntax alone does not supply semantics or validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Separating a drawn notation from a precisely defined semantics is also the route the OMG took in SysML v2, its recent standard for systems modeling, which pairs graphical and textual notations with a kernel language that has a formal semantics [@omg2025sysml].

Three findings bear on how readable BPMN diagrams are. In practice, BPMN models use a small part of the notation, on average nine kinds of element [@zurmuehlen2008language]. Comprehension of a process model declines as the model grows [@reijers2011understandability], and an analysis of BPMN's symbols against principles of notation design found several of them hard to tell apart [@moody2009physics; @genon2011cognitive].

### Machine-readable protocols in other fields

The move toward machine-readable protocols is not unique to the cognitive and behavioral sciences. Clinical research is standardizing the protocol document itself, through CDISC ODM and its study design extension [@cdisc_odm], the ICH M11 structured digital protocol [@ich2025m11], and the AI extensions SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI [@cruzrivera2020spiritai; @liu2020consortai]. In the wet lab, executable protocol languages such as Autoprotocol, LabOP, and Aquarium author and log bench procedures from one specification [@beal2022labop; @vasilev2021aquarium]. ISA-Tab structures experiment metadata for reuse [@sansone2012isa], and psychology is formalizing the analysis plan as machine-readable preregistration [@peters2023preregr]. None of these specifies an executable experiment in which the instrument may be as varied as a cognitive task and the participant may be a person or an artificial agent without a change to the protocol.

### Artificial agents and AI evaluation

The same gap has been identified within AI evaluation. Shared harnesses standardize how models are scored, among them HELM [@liang2023helm], the LM Evaluation Harness [@biderman2024lessons], BIG-bench [@srivastava2023bigbench], and Inspect [@aisi2024inspect], and new evaluation frameworks are converging on them from earlier task specifications [@metr2024taskstandard]. Agentic benchmarks now ship whole executable environments [@zhou2024webarena; @xie2024osworld; @mialon2024gaia]. Yet audits repeatedly find that what was run cannot be recovered from what was reported. None of 400 surveyed AI papers documented everything needed to reproduce them [@gundersen2018state], and an independent attempt reproduced only about 64% of 255 machine learning papers [@raff2019step]. Results shift with undocumented details of the experiments [@biderman2024lessons; @leech2024questionable], aggregate scores hide the behavior on single instances [@burnell2023rethink], and widely used benchmarks fail basic criteria of reproducibility [@reuel2024betterbench; @kapoor2025agents]. These harnesses are specifications that only developers read and only machines run. None extends to a human cohort, to eligibility criteria, or to publication figures.

Research on machine behavior has called for studying intelligent machines with the methods of behavioral science [@rahwan2019machine]. A fast-growing literature, gathered under the name of machine psychology [@hagendorff2024machinepsych], now administers psychology experiments to language models. It includes batteries of cognitive tasks [@binz2023gpt3; @codaforno2024cogbench], simulated human samples [@aher2023llms; @argyle2023silicon], comparisons of humans and models on the same tasks [@webb2023analogical; @strachan2024tom; @mei2024turing], and foundation models of cognition trained on human performance transcribed into text [@binz2025centaur]. In each case, the protocol is a custom prompting harness written anew for each paper, and the human and model administrations are matched by hand. Methodological critiques [@ivanova2025cognitive; @dillion2023replace; @lin2025fallacies], a consensus reporting checklist for studies of language models [@feuerriegel2026guidellm], and the CHART guideline for studies that evaluate chatbots [@chart2025] now call for a pinned, shareable, and executable record of how an experiment was administered. No current artifact provides such a record for a whole study. SweetBean, described above, provides it for the stimulus sequence.

The notation shows who decides what. A manual task is a step taken by a person, a language model only answers the messages that the study sends to its pool, and the decision of a gateway is a condition anyone can read. Agentic research systems draw this boundary in a separate figure [@chen2026brainresearcher], whereas in Studyflow it is part of the executable study model. They have also arrived at similar records from the other direction. Brain Researcher seals a commitment card with a content hash before an analysis runs, and afterwards writes a claim card that classifies each claim as one of six outcomes, such as accepted or rejected [@chen2026brainresearcher]. A deposited Studyflow diagram plays the role of the commitment card, and its executed diagram the role of the claim card. The diagram differs in two ways. It is executable and can render the figure, and it spans the whole study lifecycle from consent to reporting.

For AI evaluation, a benchmark and its human baseline can become one auditable artifact. Rankings built on a single task are fragile [@dehghani2021lottery], and psychometric evaluation calls for a battery of tasks varied in a controlled way [@wang2026psychometrics; @bean2025construct], whereas agentic benchmarks typically collect their human baselines outside the process that the experimental design defines [@mialon2024gaia]. A diagram would then sit beside model cards, evaluation cards, and datasheets [@mitchell2019modelcards; @dhar2025evalcards; @gebru2021datasheets] as an evaluation card that a third party can run as well as read, as independent audits require [@raji2022outsider]. The checklists proposed for studies of language models and for AI benchmarks [@feuerriegel2026guidellm; @reuel2024betterbench; @zhu2025abc] add items on the model, the prompts, and the settings [@chart2025], which one diagram would carry for human and artificial cohorts alike.

### Summary

Each body of work covers part of a study. Workflow engines run analyses, experiment builders and orchestration platforms run tasks and sessions, reporting guidelines and data standards describe the report and the data, provenance standards record what was run, and visual notations draw processes for people to read. Evaluation harnesses do the same for artificial agents, without a human cohort. None of them holds the whole study, from eligibility and allocation through the analysis to the published figure, as one artifact that people can read and machines can run, for human and artificial participants alike. Studyflow is designed to fill that gap, and it calls the tools reviewed here rather than replacing them.

@reltbl-principles pairs each documented problem with the principle it implies and with the part of this paper that examines it.

::: {#reltbl-principles}

| Problem in current practice | Design principle | Where this paper examines it |
|:-------|:----|:----|
| Each stage keeps its own copy of the study's parameters, and the copies drift apart; reports depart from registered plans without saying so [@goldacre2019compare; @claesen2021adherence] | One authoritative description, from which protocol, analysis plan, record, and figures are derived | Deviations found by comparing a changed study with the original (@tbl-blind) |
| A plan in prose leaves decisions open, and checking adherence takes human judgment [@bakker2020preregistrations; @hardwicke2023preregistration] | People read the description that the software runs | Registered decision rules and their outcomes in simulated runs (@tbl-rule, @tbl-planted) |
| Analysts read prose in different ways, and code is closed to most readers [@silberzahn2018manyanalysts; @botviniknezer2020variability] | Readable without programming, with one meaning for a machine | Views of one diagram for different readers (@fig-views); readability not yet measured (Limitations) |
| Research processes have no shared standard, and their documentation is often too incomplete to repeat them [@aguilar2022experiments; @nosek2022replicability] | Build on a process standard and community data standards, not a new format | Export to valid BPMN 2.0; datasets bound to community schemas (Materials and methods) |
| Shared data alone often do not let others reproduce a study's results [@hardwicke2018cognition; @cruwell2023badge] | Describe the process and its data in one artifact | Analysis checked against the declared data before the run (@fig-step3-analyze) |
| Each tool covers part of a study, and the artifacts of different tools are not linked (sections above) | Call task and analysis software instead of replacing it; extend the notation without changing its core | Tasks from two toolkits in one study (@fig-step2-run) |
| Studies with artificial agents re-implement the protocol each time and match human and model administrations by hand [e.g., @binz2023gpt3; @codaforno2024cogbench] | One protocol for any participant, human or artificial | Variants of the example study that differ only in the agent (@lst-swap) |

Problems in current practice reported in the literature (sections above), the principle each implies for the design of a study description, and the part of this paper that examines it.
:::
